content:
Even with zero Primary 1 classes, we must become an upgraded version of an estate school

Before the merger, SKH Tseung Kwan O Kei Tak Primary School had already adopted a "counter-cyclical" strategy. Principal Kwong Ka-man said the school would invest HK$1.8 million in the new academic year to enrich students' diverse learning experiences. The school football pitch will be opened for students to ride bicycles, and the school will provide free enhanced physical training, subsidise all students to learn swimming, and strengthen the English curriculum.

The principal said: "Even with zero Primary 1 classes, we must build the best school and become an upgraded version of an estate school." This HK$1.8 million funding mainly comes from private cars?

On the first day of the new term, students who had just moved up a level had mixed feelings. A student surnamed Ng, knowing the school would close due to insufficient enrolment, said: "I am both happy and unhappy. I'm happy because there may be more students in the future and the campus will be livelier; I'm unhappy because such a big school is gone just like that — it's hard to accept."

The most unforgettable thing is the "Kei Tak" classrooms

Recalling her days at Tseung Kwan O Kei Tak Primary School, student Ng said the most unforgettable experience was an exchange study tour to Xi'an with teachers and classmates. Another student surnamed Wong described how teachers made learning fun, using games to help students learn. She hoped the Wong Tai Sin school would have teachers as good as those at Kei Tak, and said what she would miss most was the "Kei Tak" classrooms, "because that's where my friends are." Student surnamed Choi said: "Having studied at Kei Tak for several years, the school suddenly disappearing is indeed a bit sad."

Resources can be concentrated on existing students

Parents' feelings were equally mixed. Ms. Au, whose son is in Primary 6, said she felt "a bit sad" and shocked upon hearing the news of zero classes. She said: "The principal just took office, and the school has been working very hard, but this year 15 primary schools are facing closure." She pointed out that the relationships built over many years between parents, the school and the teaching team allowed everyone to adjust quickly, adding that "there are gains and losses," and "since this is God's arrangement," she instead saw her child facing adversity more positively. The school could also concentrate resources on existing students, no longer constrained by enrolment issues.

"The school is just unable to attract enough students — why must it be forced to merge?"

Mrs. Ng has a Primary 4 child and another son who has already graduated. She said her child felt the school had "more care" upon returning, and really liked the teachers and principal. She said: "When I first received the closure news, I was really at a loss. Such a good school, just unable to attract enough students — why must it be forced to merge?" What she appreciated most about Kei Tak was that it gave children confidence, something "children today really lack" — her child is not afraid of anything.

Concerned about cross-district schooling in the future

Mrs. Wang has children in Primary 4 and Primary 6. She admitted she was of course unhappy at first, feeling it was "not worth it." Mrs. Wang said: "The school is so good, the children learn so happily — why don't other people know about it?" After adjusting her mindset, she saw "opportunity in danger." While the merger "may not be the ideal outcome," from March this year until now, she had seen the school invite all teachers and students to walk this path together, and her children had also learned to face difficulties and challenges collectively. She was grateful for Kei Tak's close home-school relationship, saying: "We are not fighting alone."

Mrs. Chung, who lives near the school, was more concerned about cross-district schooling in the future. She said the ideal would of course be to stay at Kei Tak, as "we all live quite close," normally just a five to ten-minute walk to school. After the merger plan was announced, she took a bus to visit the Wong Tai Sin school, finding it "acceptable" — about a 20-minute bus ride followed by a short walk.

Strong sense of belonging to "Kei Tak"

She once asked her daughter whether she wanted to transfer to another primary school in the same district. Her daughter replied: "I don't want to leave this school," showing her strong sense of belonging to "Kei Tak." Mrs. Chung respected her daughter's choice and would accompany her through the transition. The school mentioned possible school bus and uniform subsidies in the future, but details have yet to be finalised. Mrs. Chung believed that crossing districts to Wong Tai Sin might mean more school net options for future secondary school placement, "taking it as an opportunity for her to step out of this district." She also mentioned that class sizes were currently very small, and after moving to Wong Tai Sin classes might be larger, requiring readjustment. However, she trusted that her daughter had learned independence at Kei Tak, so she was "not too worried."

Principal: focused on doing well in the future

Principal Kwong Ka-man, herself an alumna, frankly admitted that having zero classes "is not good news for the school," but the key was how to transform it: "We are focused on doing well in the future." She did not want to tell a tragic story, noting that "in fact we are all very positive." The news was not announced today, and teachers and students had had time to process it.

After Primary 6 graduates left, Kei Tak has 121 students this academic year, and has admitted six transfer students — one in Primary 2, four in Primary 5, and one in Primary 6. Kwong Ka-man said the overall student attrition rate from Primary 2 to Primary 6 was similar to previous years, with about ten students leaving during the summer, two due to relocation and the rest transferring to other districts.

Formerly the Wong Tai Sin Kei Tak AM school

Asked whether the merger news had "scared away" students, she said it could not be generalised. She pointed out that the secondary school net in Sai Kung District was ultimately less attractive than Kwun Tong or "the other side of Kowloon." "When there are not enough students across the whole city, it's like musical chairs — they keep moving around." Some parents, even before their children left, still had great confidence in the school, simply saying they wanted to move to other districts for schooling.

"Kei Tak" was formerly the Wong Tai Sin Kei Tak AM school. In 2004, the government allocated a Tseung Kwan O school premises, and the two schools later split into whole-day schools. Kwong Ka-man said the Wong Tai Sin school "is in fact our alma mater," with the same sponsoring body and shared origins, making the merger easier to handle. Over the next three years, the school will gradually increase joint activities, collaborative lesson preparation and teaching research between the two schools' students, so that students needing to transfer schools in three years' time can adapt more easily.

Allocation based on Wong Tai Sin school net after graduation

The Education Bureau provides up to HK$1 million in配套 funding per merger case, with details such as school bus subsidies still being finalised. She acknowledged that some parents felt the distance was too far and wanted to stay in Tseung Kwan O; but from another perspective, after graduation students would be allocated places under the Wong Tai Sin school net, potentially offering options such as Kowloon City. Most parents are currently in a "cautious观望" state.

Among the 15 schools with zero Primary 1 classes, eight will merge, including SKH Tseung Kwan O Kei Tak Primary School and Wong Tai Sin SKH Kei Tak Primary School. The two schools will merge across districts, expected to be completed in the 2029–2030 academic year. Another four will close, two will operate private Primary 1 classes, and one will continue to participate in Primary 1 allocation.
